implementation_notes: asyncio.gather(*parts) is the stdlib wait-for-all aggregator: it returns the results in argument order once the last awaitable finishes, and asyncio.TaskGroup (3.11+) adds structured cancellation; asyncio.as_completed or concurrent.futures.as_completed with a ThreadPoolExecutor give the completion-order form needed for time-out and best-so-far strategies. The classic collector object is still required when partials arrive from a broker rather than being spawnable tasks: a dict keyed by correlation id plus a counter and an asyncio.timeout/loop.call_later expiry is the stateful filter, because gather knows nothing about message identity or de-duplication.
code_sketch:
async def best_quote(vendors: list[str]) -> Quote:
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:          # fans out, cancels siblings
        tasks = [tg.create_task(ask(v)) for v in vendors]
    return min((t.result() for t in tasks), key=lambda q: q.rate)
pitfalls: gather(return_exceptions=False) raises the first exception while the siblings keep running, so orphaned tasks can mutate shared state after the aggregate was abandoned - use return_exceptions=True or a TaskGroup.
Asyncio is single-threaded: one blocking call inside a gathered coroutine stalls every other partial (use asyncio.to_thread or a ThreadPoolExecutor).
A correlation-keyed collector must expire entries (asyncio.timeout/call_later) and pop them on both completion and timeout, or one lost message leaks state forever.
